interest: This document provides tangible administrative evidence of the pre-World War II economic disengagement between Japan and the United States in the autumn of 1940, amidst escalating diplomatic tensions following Japan's signing of the Tripartite Pact and tightening U.S. commercial restrictions. It highlights the role of state-level regulators, specifically the New York State Insurance Department under Louis H. Pink, in tracking the curtailment of Japanese commercial activities—here, the cessation of fire insurance underwriting by the U.S. branches of major firms Tokio Marine and Meiji Fire. For historians of international economic relations and wartime economic mobilization, it documents the incremental withdrawal and surveillance of Japanese financial entities in the United States prior to the comprehensive freezing of Japanese assets in July 1941.
keywords: Tokio Marine and Fire Insurance Company
overview: This file consists of a single State Department cross-reference sheet (decimal file 894.5061/9), dated October 7, 1940, indexing a letter from Louis H. Pink of the New York State Insurance Department originally filed under decimal number 894.506/10. The referenced communication conveys data concerning the discontinuance of the writing of fire insurance business in the United States by the American branches of two major Japanese insurance corporations, the Tokio Marine and Fire Insurance Company, Ltd., and the Meiji Fire Insurance Company, Ltd., reflecting the contraction of Japanese commercial activities in the U.S. during late 1940.
